content: The United States National Library of Medicine (NLM), operated by the federal government, is recognized as the largest medical library in the world. Its extensive collections encompass over seven million items, including books, journals, technical reports, manuscripts, microfilms, photographs, and images related to medicine and the sciences. These collections also include some of the oldest and rarest works in the field. Since 1879, the NLM has been responsible for publishing the Index Medicus, a monthly guide to articles from nearly 5,000 selected journals. This resource includes approximately five million references, with records dating back to the 1950s. The NLM also oversees the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), which provides access to biological databases through the Entrez search engine and PubMed. These resources are freely available online. In 1967, the NLM established the Toxicology and Environmental Health Program (TEHIP), which focuses on developing computer databases derived from medical literature and data from governmental and non-governmental organizations. TEHIP has implemented several information systems designed for chemical emergency response and public education, including the Toxicology Data Network (TOXNET), TOXMAP, Tox Town, the Wireless Information System for Emergency Responders (WISER), ToxMystery, and the Household Products Database. All of these resources are accessible free of charge via the internet. The Extramural Programs Division of the NLM provides grants to support research in medical information science and the development of computer and communication systems for use in medical institutions. Additionally, the division supports research and publications in the history of medicine and life sciences. The origins of the NLM can be traced back to the establishment of the Army Medical Museum in 1862, which later became the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology and its Medical Museum. Historically, the Army Medical Library and the Army Medical Museum often shared facilities. Between 1866 and 1887, they were housed in Ford's Theatre after it ceased theatrical productions following the assassination of President Abraham Lincoln. In 1956, the library was transferred from the Department of Defense to the Public Health Service under the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, and it was renamed the National Library of Medicine. In 1962, the library relocated to its current location on the campus of the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland.
